scope.q: What specific data points or characteristics define the 'patterns' the fraud team is currently identifying, and how are these patterns currently being surfaced or communicated?
scope.why: Understanding the precise nature of the 'signal' and its current manual processing is critical for designing effective data ingestion and automation.

scope.q: What is the target timeframe for intervention once a potential fraudulent pattern is detected, and what are the precise actions the system should be able to initiate or recommend?
scope.why: Defining 'fast enough' and the specific actions (e.g., block, flag, review) quantifies the performance requirements and the system's operational output.

scope.q: What is the acceptable false positive rate for any automated fraud prevention action, considering the potential impact on legitimate customer transactions and experience?
scope.why: This directly quantifies the risk tolerance and informs model design, thresholding, and the critical balance between fraud prevention and user friction.

decomposition.title: Data Ingestion & Feature Store Development
decomposition.why: We need to reliably collect, clean, and transform raw transaction and user data into a consistent, usable format for detection models.

decomposition.title: Real-time Pattern Detection Service
decomposition.why: This core component will host and execute the fraud detection logic, identifying suspicious activities based on ingested features and trained models.

decomposition.title: Action Orchestration & Workflow Integration
decomposition.why: The system needs to translate detection events into concrete, configurable actions that integrate with existing fraud team processes and external systems.

decomposition.title: Feedback Loop & Model Retraining Pipeline
decomposition.why: Continuous improvement requires capturing outcomes of actions and human analyst feedback, then using this to automatically retrain and update detection models.

decomposition.title: Fraud Analyst User Interface
decomposition.why: Analysts require a dedicated tool to review alerts, investigate cases, provide feedback, and manage model configurations and rules.

sprint.title: Data Source Integration & Staging
sprint.deliv: Working pipeline ingesting raw transaction data from a primary source into a staging database.

sprint.title: Core Feature Engineering & Feature Store
sprint.deliv: Initial set of 5-10 calculated features (e.g., transaction velocity, amount variance) from raw data, stored in a basic feature store.

sprint.title: Basic Rule-Based Detection Service
sprint.deliv: A service that applies 2-3 predefined, simple fraud rules on features and logs detected alerts to a temporary store.

sprint.title: Action Orchestration MVP
sprint.deliv: A service that receives a rule-based alert and can trigger a configurable external API call (e.g., log to an internal communication tool like Slack or Jira).

sprint.title: Fraud Analyst UI Stub
sprint.deliv: A basic web interface showing a list of triggered alerts from the detection service with minimal transaction details.

sprint.title: Feedback Loop & Data Capture
sprint.deliv: Mechanism within the UI for analysts to mark alerts as 'true fraud' or 'false positive', storing this feedback in a database.

sprint.title: Model Training Proof-of-Concept
sprint.deliv: An offline script demonstrating training a simple ML model (e.g., Logistic Regression) using historical features and captured feedback data.

risks.risk: Incomplete or inconsistent historical transaction data leads to poor model training and unreliable feature generation.
risks.mitigation: Conduct a thorough data audit with the fraud team in week 1, establishing clear data ownership and defining data quality gates for ingestion pipelines.

risks.risk: High false positive rate from automated detection leads to legitimate customer transactions being blocked, causing revenue loss and customer dissatisfaction.
risks.mitigation: Implement A/B testing or shadow mode deployment for new detection models, allowing performance monitoring against actual fraud team decisions before full activation, and setting clear, adjustable confidence thresholds.

risks.risk: Integration with various legacy external systems (e.g., payment gateways, CRM) for taking action proves more complex and time-consuming than anticipated.
risks.mitigation: Prioritize integration with the single most impactful action system first, building a generic action orchestration layer that abstracts specific API calls, and plan for phased rollout of additional integrations.

risks.risk: Fraudsters adapt quickly, rendering static detection patterns or models obsolete, leading to a resurgence in chargebacks.
risks.mitigation: Establish a continuous feedback loop and automated model retraining pipeline (e.g., weekly or bi-weekly), incorporating analyst feedback and new fraud patterns, with robust model versioning and monitoring for performance degradation.
